title: Theology is one science by species under divine revelation, and is practical rather than merely speculative
pass_a_gloss: Further Theology science-is one by-species, not multiplex. Although it-treats of-things very diverse (God, Angels, man, virtues and vices seeming to-belong to diverse sciences), all nevertheless agree in one common reason under which they-are-objected to-Theology: divine revelation. pass_b_english: Further, theology is one science by species, not many. For although it treats of things that are very diverse — for example, of God, of angels, of man, of virtues and vices, which seem to belong to altogether different sciences — still all those things agree in one common formal reason, under which they confront and are objected to theology. That common reason is divine revelation. For the things I have named do not fall under the theologian's consideration in any way whatever, but only insofar as they can be known through divine revelation. For example, concerning the nature, powers, and duty of man the theologian does not teach whatever can be taught, but only those things which he has learned and gathered from the word of God.

Here it must also be noted that not whatever God reveals in any manner whatever pertains to the object of theology. For God may have revealed certain things privately to many persons, which do not fall under this science. But here by revelation we understand that which is common to the whole church, and which was made for its common usefulness, and which God willed to be consigned in writing. For the theologian ought to prove his assertions not from private revelations made to this person or that, but from sacred Scripture.

Further, theology does not seem to be a science merely speculative, nor merely practical, but practical and speculative at once. And that is because theology treats of many things that belong to practical science as well as to speculative. For it contemplates God and the divine mysteries, which do not fall under action; and it also gives precepts of life, and teaches what manners are worthy of a Christian man.

Nevertheless we judge theology to be practical rather than speculative. For the whole of theology is occupied in the explanation and defense of the things contained in the Scriptures. But the teaching contained in the Scriptures, from the scope of God himself who teaches and reveals, is referred to action — namely to the love of God and of neighbor. Nor has anyone attained the scope of this teaching who does not refer whatever he has learned from the word of God to that end. For Christ affirms in ([[Matthew 22:37-40 >> Bible:Matthew 22:37-40]]) that the law and the prophets hang on these two commandments: you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and your neighbor as yourself. Then Paul says in ([[Romans 15:4 >> Bible:Romans 15:4]]) that whatever things were written were written for our learning, that through patience and the comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope. But above all his words in ([[2 Timothy 3:16-17 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16-17]]) are to be weighed: All Scripture is inspired by God, and is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for discipline which is in righteousness; that the man of God may be perfect, and thoroughly furnished unto every good work.

To this belongs the fact that the Gospel is called by the same Paul a teaching according to godliness ([[1 Timothy 6:3 >> Bible:1 Timothy 6:3]]). For that is for no other reason than that the chief scope of the Gospel is to form us unto godliness. Indeed those articles which seem most to pertain to contemplation — namely concerning the divinity and incarnation of the Son of God — are called by the Apostle in specie the mystery of godliness, in chapter 3 of the same epistle ([[1 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:1 Timothy 3:16]]). Add that the habit of the theological principles is faith. But true faith is a practical habit. And the habit of the principles and the habit of the conclusions are of the same genus.
source_text:
XVI. Porro Theologia scientia est una specie, non multiplex. Licet enim de rebus valde diversis agat, exempli gratia, de Deo, de Angelis, de homine, de virtutibus et vitiis, quae videntur ad prorsus diversas scientias pertinere, omnia tamen illa in una ratione communi conveniunt, sub qua Theologiae obversantur et objiciuntur. Quae ratio communis est revelatio divina. Ista enim quae dixi non quovis modo cadunt sub Theologi considerationem: sed quatenus per divinam revelationem cognosci possunt. Nam verbi causa, de natura, viribus et officio hominis non docet Theologus quaecunque doceri possunt, sed ea tantum quae ex verbo Dei didicit et collegit.

XVII. Est autem hic notandum, non quaecunque Deus quovis modo revelat ad Theologiae objectum pertinere. Potest enim Deus multis quaedam privatim revelasse, quae non cadunt sub hanc scientiam. Sed hic per revelationem intelligimus illam, quae Ecclesiae toti communis est, et in communem ejus utilitatem est facta, quamque Deus scriptis voluit consignari. Siquidem non ex privatis revelationibus huic aut illi factis, sed ex Scriptura sacra, assertiones suas probare debet Theologus.

XVIII. Porro Theologia non videtur esse scientia mere speculativa, neque mere practica, sed practica simul et speculativa. Et hoc quia Theologia de multis rebus agit, quae spectant ad scientiam tam practicam, quam speculativam. Deum enim contemplatur et mysteria divina, quae sub actionem non cadunt: tum quoque vitae praecepta dat, docetque qui sint mores homine Christiano digni.

XIX. Verumtamen Theologiam censemus potius esse practicam quam speculativam. Siquidem universa Theologia versatur in explicatione, et defensione eorum quae continentur in Scripturis. Atqui doctrina in Scripturis contenta, ex ipsius Dei docentis et revelantis scopo, ad actionem refertur, videlicet ad Dei et proximi dilectionem. Neque doctrinae hujus scopum assecutus est, qui non quaecunque ex verbo Dei didicit, ad finem illum refert. Affirmat enim Christus Matth. 22. legem atque Prophetas pendere ex his duobus mandatis, nempe, Dominum Deum tuum diliges toto corde, et tota anima, et proximum sicut teipsum. Deinde dicit Paulus Rom. 15. Quaecunque scripta sunt ad nostram doctrinam scripta esse, ut per patientiam, et consolationem Scripturarum spem habeamus. Sed praesertim maxime ponderanda sunt ejus verba, 2. Tim. 3. Tota Scriptura divinitus inspirata, utilis est ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad disciplinam quae est in justitia; ut perfectus sit homo Dei, et ad omne bonum opus perfecte instructus.

XX. Huc facit, quod Evangelium ab eodem Paulo dicitur doctrina quae est secundum pietatem, 1 Tim. 6. Hoc enim aliunde non est, nisi quod praecipuus Evangelii scopus, est nos ad pietatem formare. Imo articuli illi qui maxime videntur pertinere ad contemplationem, nimirum de filii Dei divinitate et incarnatione, mysterium pietatis ab Apostolo dicuntur in specie, cap. 3. ejusdem Epistolae. Adde quod Theologicorum principiorum habitus est fides. At vera fides habitus est practicus. Ejusdem vero generis est habitus principiorum, et habitus conclusionum.
